newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi says opposition rallies to be allowed.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi says opposition rallies to be allowed.

text.p: Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi has said opposition parties would automatically be granted official licences for rallies in most cases, his second apparent concession under pressure from a political reform campaign.

But opposition leaders pressing for reforms before a general election this year said Moi should dismantle the law requiring licences which run counter to the right of free assembly in the constitution.

The official Presidential Press Service quoted the president as telling a rally southeast of Nairobi on Wednesday licences would be denied only in exceptional circumstances and reasons would be given.
He said his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party and the opposition were therefore free to hold rallies under the Public Order Act, which the opposition demands be scrapped.
Moi said a decision to grant licences for rallies was taken as the government-sponsored Peaceful Assemblies Act, superseding the Public Order Act, had not yet been passed by parliament.
Michael Kijana Wamalwa, the opposition leader in parliament who met Moi for 10 minutes on Wednesday, welcomed his latest apparent concession but said the Public Order Act still had to be repealed.
Opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies spearheading the campaign for reforms before elections have held a string of rallies since June without applying for licences.
Riot police on July 7 violently broke up rallies in Nairobi and several other cities and towns and at least nine people were killed in the worst political violence in Kenya in seven years.
The July 7 violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by days of student unrest in the city, prompting the closure of two universities followed by the Kenya Polytechnic on Monday.

On Wednesday, Moi agreed to Wamalwa's request to meet opposition leaders next week to discuss constitutional reforms. But the president has said there was not enough time for them before presidential and parliamentary elections this year.

Moi on Tuesday met church leaders and agreed on the need for a review of the constitution. But some members of the National Convention Executive Council (NCEC), leading the drive for reforms, accused him of attempting to divide the opposition.
They said the meeting was no concession as it featured religious leaders who backed the president and was part of a new political offensive by Moi to divide reform groups and scuttle their campaign.
The independent Daily Nation newspaper said on Thursday clerics at Tuesday's meeting believed Moi was only trying to buy time and soften the government's image of intransigence.
But the Nation called Moi's decision on Wednesday to grant most licences for political rallies "another key concession".

It said the NCEC planned an overnight vigil on Thursday night at offices in Nairobi for 14 people the committee says were killed in the clashes with police on July 7. It said an open-air service would be held in a Nairobi park on Friday.
The opposition says religious services do not require licences.
The constitutional reforms sought by the opposition would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and Kenya's ruler for 19 years. No date for the presidential and parliamentary polls has been set.
The NCEC says unless it reaches an agreement with Moi on reforms the next target of its campaign will be the Indian Ocean port city of Mombasa, the centre of Kenya's tourism industry.
